sources.title: New forensic evidence supports Egyptian "retainer sacrifice"

discussion.body: The paper's author, Roselyn Campbell, is a bioarchaeologist at Purdue who studies how people decide which kinds of violence are acceptable, and how violence gets defined in the first place.

She also warns against importing our own definitions. Violence is context-specific, and Egypt's archaeology carries a long colonial legacy of outsiders arriving with fixed ideas about what the culture was.

items.title: The Egyptian Skulls That May Point to Retainer Sacrifice
items.body: A new paper in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology reassesses a collection of skulls excavated from Egyptian tombs in the 1920s. Over one-third of them show evidence of blunt force trauma — which, in the paper's reading, suggests they may have been victims of so-called retainer sacrifice, the burial of retainers alongside a dead ruler. That word 'may' is doing real work here: a pattern of healed or unhealed injuries on old bone can suggest a practice without proving one.

items.title: The Moon Rock That Also Shows Up in Madagascar
items.body: Anorthosite is common on the Moon's surface, where its light, highly reflective patches are visible from Earth with the unaided eye as the lunar highlands. It is not a Moon exclusive. The same rock crops up across Earth's surface — eastern Canada, Scandinavia, southern India — and in Madagascar, where it forms a striking round feature. It is a reminder that the bright grey we associate with the Moon is a property of a mineral, not of a place.

sources.title: APOD: 2026 October 5 – M104: The Sombrero Galaxy’s Tidal Streams

discussion.body: Deeper images get stranger: within that stellar haze, structures become visible, including a diagonal ring.
And the scale is unhelpful for intuition — light takes about 30 million years to reach us from the Sombrero, which spans roughly 150 thousand light years.

items.title: The Sombrero Galaxy Is a Hat Only in Short Exposures
items.body: M104 earns its nickname on short exposures: it looks like a hat. A much longer exposure brings up a hairy past instead, revealing a bright, hazy halo that extends well past the central disk and contains many stars the image cannot resolve. The hat is largely an artifact of how briefly we looked.

sources.title: Korea Box Office: ‘The Assassin(s)’ Holds Admissions Lead as ‘Chiikawa’ Generates Top Weekend Gross

items.title: Two Winners in One Korean Box-Office Weekend
items.body: Director Hur Jin-ho's political crime thriller “The Assassin(s)” held the top position at the South Korean box office in admissions over the Oct. 2–4 weekend, while the Japanese animated feature “Chiikawa the Movie: The Secret of the Mermaid Island” captured the frame's largest gross revenue. Two measures, two winners: a weekend can be led by the film that sold the most tickets or by the film that took the most money, and they need not be the same title.

sources.title: Brazil election: Bolsonaro and Lula head to runoff

items.title: Brazil's Presidential Race Is Headed to a Runoff, With Flávio Bolsonaro Narrowly Ahead of Lula
items.body: Brazil's presidential contest will be settled in a runoff. Deutsche Welle reports that Flávio Bolsonaro, described as a populist, has secured a thin lead over incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva — but the country's electoral court says the next president will be decided in the runoff round, not on the first count that produced that lead.

sources.title: France closes up to 500 schools Monday over student protests

items.title: France Suspends Lessons in Some High Schools After Clashes With Student Protesters
items.body: France's education minister says lessons will be “totally or partly suspended” in some high schools after clashes between riot police and student protesters, the BBC reports. Closing classrooms is a strange instrument for a government facing unrest: it removes the lesson and the gathering place at once, and it puts the education ministry, not only the police, on the front line of the dispute.

sources.title: Marvel Canceled ‘Blade,’ But the Gory Vampire Brawler ‘Half’ Will Thrill Genre Fans

discussion.body: The premise underneath the review is the interesting bit: an audience for a genre doesn't belong to the studio that shelved it. If the critic is right, a small Indian production can serve the Blade fans Marvel left waiting.
“Will bring joy” is one critic's prediction, not a measurement. Nobody has counted the joy yet.

items.title: The Vampire Brawler Marvel Didn't Make, and the Indian Film That Steps In
items.body: Variety's critic thinks Kevin Feige made a rare misstep: Marvel's architect, in this telling, “dropped the bag” by not making a new “Blade.” The consolation, per the same review, is “Half,” directed by Indian auteur Samjad — a film that will bring joy to fans of the battle-ready half-vampire Wesley Snipes popularized. The idea worth chewing on is not a scorecard of Feige's slate decisions but the claim that a fandom can be served from outside the studio system that created it: Marvel let the character sit, and a genre film from India turns up to fill the slot. Whether “Half” satisfies that appetite is a review question, not a scheduling one.

sources.title: A swordfish was found on Haida Gwaii. Will more follow?

discussion.body: The load-bearing word is “unexpected.” Rarity and surprise are different measurements, and warming waters are moving the second one faster than the first.
Which is also why one fish settles little on its own. “No longer unexpected” is a statement about ocean conditions, not evidence of a new swordfish population off Haida Gwaii.

items.title: A Swordfish on Haida Gwaii: Unusual, but No Longer Unexpected
items.body: A swordfish turned up on Haida Gwaii, and a University of British Columbia researcher says the finding is unusual but no longer unexpected, given warming waters worldwide, including in Canada. That pairing is the interesting part. One swordfish is still an anomaly; what has changed is that the anomaly now fits conditions researchers already expect. Whether more follow is the question the report itself raises.

sources.title: ‘The Social Reckoning’ New York Red Carpet Premiere Photos: Jeremy Strong, Mikey Madison, Jeremy Allen White & More

items.title: Aaron Sorkin's Facebook Leak Drama Reaches Theaters Friday
items.body: The Social Reckoning held its U.S. premiere Sunday at the Regal Union Square in New York, following earlier screenings in London and Paris, and Deadline reports the Aaron Sorkin-helmed film opens in theaters Friday. It dramatizes the 2021 Facebook leak by whistleblower Frances Haugen and Jeff Horwitz, with Mikey Madison playing Haugen. That casting choice points the story at the person who took the material out rather than at the platform it came from — an accountability drama told from the leaker's side of the desk, which is a different animal from a story about how a company got built.

sources.title: ‘Lanterns’ Finale Review: Episode 8 Makes the Hard Choices — and Leaves a Light on for Season 2

discussion.body: A finale that keeps its focus on people instead of fireworks is doing the harder job in some ways: it still has to close something, just with talk and feeling rather than a showpiece.
A dense, emotional finale with three credited writers can cut either way. Crowded can look like rich when the characters are ones you already care about.

items.title: Lanterns Ends With Feeling Rather Than Fireworks
items.body: IndieWire's review of the Lanterns finale notes that showrunner Chris Mundy wrote the episode with co-creators Damon Lindelof and Tom King, and describes it as dense and emotional, built around character rather than spectacle, with love shown in messy rather than tidy form. Three writers converging on a final hour is a bet on intimacy in a slot that usually goes big — the finale as a conversation instead of a set piece.

sources.title: In Tigray, Ethiopian government forces have advanced against a northern rebel group, reports indicate

items.title: Ethiopian Forces Advance, and the Worry Is Regional
items.body: Deutsche Welle reports that Ethiopian government forces have advanced against a northern rebel group, and that renewed fighting has raised fears the conflict could spill over into the wider region. The advance is attributed to reports rather than to a single confirmed account, and the fear DW highlights is regional: the concern is not only who holds ground in the north, but what the fighting draws in around it.

sources.title: The misperception that keeps bystanders from intervening and how to short‑circuit it

discussion.body: If the problem is a mistaken guess about other people's attitudes, then fixing the guess is a cheaper intervention than trying to change character. Beliefs about peers are things a campaign or a conversation can actually reach.

But the misperception has a comfortable payoff. Assuming everyone else is untroubled by something saves you from being the one person who objects — and the person who objects is often the one who pays a social cost.
Which is precisely why the useful move is to make the disagreement visible. If the silence is the evidence people are misreading, then breaking it is what corrects the estimate.

items.title: Bystanders May Be Reading the Room Wrong
items.body: PBS NewsHour points to a specific failure of judgment behind bystander inaction: people may accept bad behavior — even sexual assault — when they overestimate how acceptable their peers think it is. The error is about belief, not behavior. What gets misread is other people's attitudes, which means a room can stay silent while most of the people in it privately object to what is happening. The same report says there are ways to undermine that thinking and make intervention more likely, and the natural target of those efforts is the guess about what everyone else thinks rather than anybody's private conscience. The uncomfortable implication is that quiet is weak evidence of approval; it may only record what each person assumed the others believed.

sources.title: Suppliers pile pressure on government over energy bills

items.title: An Energy Trade Body Pushes for Winter Bill Relief
items.body: Energy UK, an energy trade body, says immediate action is needed to help households struggling with bills this winter, BBC Business reports. The timing is the argument: the appeal lands ahead of the cold months, when energy bills are hardest to avoid or absorb. There is no seasonal mystery in that, but there is a political logic — the closer winter gets, the harder it becomes for anyone to say the problem is someone else's to solve later. What makes the item worth a second look is who is doing the asking. When an industry's own trade body presses publicly for help with household costs, the bill problem is being treated as a shared one rather than a private hardship.

sources.title: Despair over future fuels political anxiety for college students on the cusp of adulthood

discussion.body: Restlessness is doing a lot of work in that sentence. Despair would be resignation; restlessness suggests these students haven't written the system off yet — they're impatient with it, which is a more demanding attitude than indifference.

Impatience and estrangement can look identical from the outside. Believing a system is no longer interested in helping you is already a step toward expecting nothing from it, however loudly you complain.

items.title: Students' Restlessness With a System They Doubt
items.body: PBS NewsHour reports on college students on the cusp of adulthood whose anxiety about the future is fuelling a restlessness with a national political system they worry is either no longer capable of improving their lives or no longer interested in helping. Those are two different complaints, and the difference matters. A system that can't help is a question of capacity — messy institutions, poor design, competing priorities. A system that won't help is a question of intent. The students, at least as described here, appear to be holding both at once, which is a harder position to argue from than either one alone. Anxiety, in this telling, isn't producing withdrawal so much as agitation: the word is restlessness, the mood of people who still want something from politics and doubt they will get it.

items.title: Sass Jordan's Page Announces Her Death
items.body: CBC Canada reports the death of Sass Jordan. A post on her social media page on Saturday said she died the day before, “surrounded by her loving family,” and called her an “inimitable force of nature” and an “irreplaceable being of light and joy.”

discussion.body: Presence isn't a quantity a parent gets to measure alone. Heneghan hands the audit to his sons in the first sentence.
That assumes the sons are grading the same thing he is. Two people could describe the same childhood as attentive and as absent without either of them lying.

items.title: A Father Thought He Was Present. His Sons Disagreed.
items.body: Liam Heneghan's essay in Psyche opens with a line that cuts against the shape of most parenting memoirs: he thought he was a present father; his sons said otherwise. When his granddaughter arrived, he made an offer. The disagreement is the interesting part. A father's account of his own attention is memory; his children's is a verdict, and the two can cover the same years without matching. That gap is what the essay works from.

sources.title: U.S. Marine arrested for alleged murder of a woman in Okinawa, Japan

items.title: A U.S. Marine Is Arrested on Okinawa in an Alleged Robbery and Murder
items.body: Japanese police arrested a U.S. Marine in the alleged robbery and murder of a woman on Okinawa, officials said Sunday, according to NPR. The robbery and killing are described as alleged; the arrest is the development officials announced.
